sections.markdown:
## C2 — Confusable pairs and continuation facts: reflector distances, helmet rules, electric bicycle classes, moped definition, truck size and power, rider positioning and procession extras
Confusable pairs among the sharing-the-road distances, speeds and helmet rules, plus continuation facts that complete part C; each block ties to one guide page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec05-R01 | anchor: A06
The bicycle lighting distances differ by item: the white front light must be visible from 500 feet, a rear red light or reflector shows at 600 feet in low beams, side reflectors or lights at 300 feet, and pedal or leg reflectors at 200 feet. [A06]
Why it matters: group bicycle equipment; confusable reflector distances; difficulty high.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-R02 | anchor: A06
A rear red reflector must be at least two square inches, or a rear red light may be used instead, and drivers must be able to see it in their low beams from 600 feet. [A06]
Why it matters: group bicycle equipment; difficulty medium.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-R03 | anchor: A06
Reflectors or lights worn on the rider's shoes or lower legs, or fitted to the pedals or crank arms, must show in low beams at 200 feet. [A06]
Why it matters: group bicycle equipment; confusable with the side reflector distance.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-R04 | anchor: A06
Reflective material or lights on each side of the bicycle or rider must show in low beams at 300 feet, a rule that does not cover mopeds meeting federal NHTSA standards. [A06]
Why it matters: group bicycle equipment; confusable with the pedal reflector distance.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-R05 | anchor: A05
For moped and bicycle riders a safety-certified helmet is advice, not a legal requirement, since state law does not demand one. [A05]
Why it matters: group helmets; confusable with the motorcycle helmet requirement on the motorcycle page; difficulty high.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-R06 | anchor: A06
Electric bicycle classes one and three both assist only while the rider pedals, but class one stops assisting at twenty mph and class three at twenty-eight mph. [A06]
Why it matters: group electric bicycles; confusable class one versus class three; difficulty high.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-R07 | anchor: A06
A class two electric bicycle uses its motor alone to move the bike and cannot assist once the bike reaches twenty mph. [A06]
Why it matters: group electric bicycles; confusable with class one.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-R08 | anchor: A06
Under the state definition an electric bicycle has working pedals, a seat or saddle, and an electric motor under 750 watts. [A06]
Why it matters: group electric bicycles; glossary electric bicycle.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-R09 | anchor: A05
A motorized bicycle, such as a moped, has two or three wheels, an automatic transmission and a motor of no more than 50 cubic centimeters producing under three gross brake horsepower. [A05]
Why it matters: group mopeds; glossary motorized bicycle; difficulty medium.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-R10 | anchor: A06
To count as a motorized bicycle, the device can go no faster than 30 mph on level ground. [A06]
Why it matters: group mopeds; confusable with the electric bicycle assist speeds.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-R11 | anchor: A01
At intersections a motorcycle rider should not count on having the right-of-way, because drivers may not see the bike or may think it is moving slower than it is. [A01]
Why it matters: group rider safety; confusable with the bicycle intersection tip; difficulty medium.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-R12 | anchor: A02
On busy intercity routes, double and triple trailer rigs can run longer than 100 feet. [A02]
Why it matters: group trucks; confusable with the ninety-foot combination length.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-R13 | anchor: A02
A loaded semi speeds up slowly: it may shift through ten gears to reach the limit, and its engine moves 30 to 40 times the weight a car engine does. [A02]
Why it matters: group trucks; difficulty low.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-R14 | anchor: A01
On residential streets with parked cars, keep at or under the speed limit, adjusting to how far ahead you can see. [A01]
Why it matters: group motorcycles; difficulty low.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-R15 | anchor: A01
Motorcycle riders should wear bright clothing, stay out of blind spots, use proper lights and reflectors at night, and signal and scan before slowing, merging or turning. [A01]
Why it matters: group rider safety; continuation of motorcycle tips.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-R16 | anchor: A03
A pedestrian should not stand in a traffic lane talking to a driver, but should wait for the car to park safely and stay on its curb side. [A03]
Why it matters: group pedestrians; difficulty low.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-R17 | anchor: A04
When getting ready to turn right, especially on a red light, watch for pedestrians and cyclists coming up on your right. [A04]
Why it matters: group pedestrians; continuation of crosswalk rules.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-R18 | anchor: A04
Look for passing cyclists before you open a car door into a traffic lane or bike lane. [A04]
Why it matters: group bicycles; difficulty low.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-R19 | anchor: A05
The right edge of a road often holds ditches, gutters, sand and gravel shoulders, so riders should leave room between themselves and those hazards. [A05]
Why it matters: group rider positioning; continuation of where to ride.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-R20 | anchor: A05
On a one-way street a bicyclist may ride as far left as is safe, and riders should check traffic and signal before shifting lanes or position. [A05]
Why it matters: group rider positioning; confusable with the keep-right default.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-R21 | anchor: A05
In heavy traffic, a less experienced cyclist may find it easier to wait near the curb until a safe gap opens. [A05]
Why it matters: group rider positioning; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-R22 | anchor: A05
For teen and adult cyclists, riding in the street with traffic is far safer than riding on the sidewalk. [A05]
Why it matters: group rider positioning; misconception sidewalk riding is safer.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-R23 | anchor: A06
Crashes between bicycles and cars climb sharply between sunset and sunrise, and proper lights and reflectors can prevent almost all of them. [A06]
Why it matters: group bicycle equipment; why the lighting rules exist.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-R24 | anchor: A07
A driver not in a funeral procession may enter an intersection the procession is crossing on a red light only without crossing the procession's path. [A07]
Why it matters: group funeral processions; continuation of the procession rules.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec05-R25 | anchor: A07
Examples of road-rage behavior include honking, flashing headlights, tailgating, chasing another car, aggressive gestures, sudden braking, deliberate blocking, cutting off and assault. [A07]
Why it matters: group road rage; difficulty low.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec05-R26 | anchor: A07
Road rage habits can be unlearned, but doing so takes self-discipline from the driver. [A07]
Why it matters: group road rage; difficulty low.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec05-R27 | anchor: A07
A lit cigarette tossed from a car window can blow into the vehicle behind and cause damage or injury, which is one reason littering is illegal. [A07]
Why it matters: group littering; difficulty low.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0036]
